verdicts.notes: Two searches. Barkley, Koplowitz, Anderson & McMurray 1997 is real (J Int Neuropsychol Soc, pp. 359-369, DOI 10.1017/S1355617797003597, PMID 9260445): two studies, Study 1 had 12 ADHD children and 26 controls aged 6-14 reproducing 12/24/36/48/60 s intervals, and it is described as the most replicated timing paradigm in ADHD research. Barkley, Murphy & Bush 2001 (Neuropsychology 15:351-360, PMID 11499990) is also real: 104 adults with ADHD vs 64 controls; ADHD group gave larger verbal estimates especially at long intervals, made shorter reproductions at 15 and 60 s and larger reproduction errors at 12, 45 and 60 s, unaffected by subtype or gender. What the summaries did not show: the 1997 results on distraction and stimulant medication, so the 'worse under distraction' and 'medication partly helped' parts of the claim are unverified; the core 'worse at reproducing time, more so at longer intervals' is confirmed by the 2001 data.
verdicts.corrected_source: Barkley RA, Koplowitz S, Anderson T, McMurray MB (1997) Sense of time in children with ADHD: effects of duration, distraction, and stimulant medication. J Int Neuropsychol Soc 3(4):359-369 (PMID 9260445). Barkley RA, Murphy KR, Bush T (2001) Time perception and reproduction in young adults with ADHD. Neuropsychology 15(3):351-360 (PMID 11499990).
verdicts.corrected_numbers: 1997 Study 1: n=12 ADHD, n=26 controls, ages 6-14, intervals 12-60 s (sample sizes were not in the claim). 2001: n=104 ADHD adults vs n=64 controls; shorter reproductions at 15 and 60 s, greater reproduction errors at 12, 45 and 60 s; larger verbal estimates at long intervals. 1997 distraction/medication direction not visible in search summaries.

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Buehler, Griffin & Ross 1994 is real (J Pers Soc Psychol 67(3):366-381; full text on MIT server). Study 1: 37 psychology honours-thesis students predicted a mean 33.9 days and took a mean 55.5 days; only about 30% finished by their predicted date; even the 'if everything goes as badly as it could' estimate (48.6 days) was shorter than the actual mean. The claim's 'about 34 vs about 56 days' and 'fewer than a third' match. The ADHD lead the researcher could not recall is also real: Prevatt, Proctor, Baker, Garrett & Yelland 2011, Time Estimation Abilities of College Students With ADHD, J Atten Disord (20 ADHD vs 20 non-ADHD college students; ADHD group differed on all measures except confidence and errors, and a secondary summary reports they over-estimated time intervals and were less accurate). No ADHD sample in the 1994 study, as the claim says.
verdicts.corrected_source: Buehler R, Griffin D, Ross M (1994) Exploring the 'planning fallacy': Why people underestimate their task completion times. J Pers Soc Psychol 67(3):366-381. ADHD follow-up: Prevatt F et al. (2011) Time Estimation Abilities of College Students With ADHD. J Atten Disord, DOI 10.1177/1087054710370673.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: n=37 students; predicted 33.9 days (best case 27.4, worst case 48.6); actual 55.5 days; ~30% finished by predicted date. Prevatt 2011: n=20 ADHD vs n=20 controls, ADHD less accurate and (per secondary summary) over-estimated; direction seen only in a secondary source, not the abstract.

verdicts.notes: Three searches. The cited single-case source checks out: Amato-Zech, Hoff & Doepke 2006, Psychology in the Schools (DOI 10.1002/pits.20137), 3 elementary-aged students in a special education classroom, ABAB reversal, MotivAider vibrating prompt, on-task behaviour rose from a mean of 55% to more than 90% of intervals; not an ADHD-only sample, as the claim says. But the claim's central assertion that no randomised or controlled trial of a visual timer exists in an ADHD sample is contradicted: Wennberg et al. 2018, 'Effectiveness of time-related interventions in children with ADHD aged 9-15 years: a randomized controlled study', European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry 27(3):329-342, is a randomised trial of time-assistive devices plus time-management intervention in exactly this age group (results not visible in the summary, and the intervention is a package rather than a bare timer). A 2025 counterbalanced within-subject study (PMC12731990, 44 children aged 7-9, timed maths assessment with and without a Time Timer) found lower anticipatory anxiety and fewer inattentive/motor-instability behaviours with the timer, strongest in children at higher ADHD risk on the Conners, with no change in maths score. So 'consensus only' understates the evidence; the recommendation to use the timer calmly as a self-check cue is not undermined.
verdicts.corrected_source: Amato-Zech NA, Hoff KE, Doepke KJ (2006) Increasing on-task behavior in the classroom: extension of self-monitoring strategies. Psychology in the Schools 43(2). Plus: Wennberg B, Janeslatt G, Kottorp A, Gustafsson PA (2018) Effectiveness of time-related interventions in children with ADHD aged 9-15 years: a randomized controlled study. Eur Child Adolesc Psychiatry 27(3):329-342; and the 2025 Time-Timer study at PMC12731990.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: Amato-Zech: n=3, 55% to >90% on-task (matches). Wennberg 2018: RCT, ADHD ages 9-15, effect sizes not seen. 2025 Time-Timer study: n=44, ages 7-9, within-subject; lower anxiety and fewer inattentive behaviours, no maths-performance difference.

verdicts.notes: One search. Knight, Sartini & Spriggs 2015 is real (J Autism Dev Disord 45:157-178, DOI 10.1007/s10803-014-2201-z, PMID 25081593), a review of 1993-2013 literature concluding that visual activity schedules can be considered an evidence-based practice for individuals with ASD, especially when combined with systematic instructional procedures. The claim's number is wrong: 31 studies met inclusion criteria but only 16 met the quality standard, not '31 met quality standards'. The summary described outcomes as 'various behaviors', so the claim's 'on-task and transition behaviour' was not specifically confirmed. The negative half of the claim (no ADHD trial of a checklist alone) was not searched within budget and remains the researcher's belief.
verdicts.corrected_source: Knight V, Sartini E, Spriggs AD (2015) Evaluating visual activity schedules as evidence-based practice for individuals with autism spectrum disorders. J Autism Dev Disord 45(1):157-178.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: 31 studies met inclusion; 16 met acceptable quality (claim said 31 met quality standards). EBP conclusion applies 'especially when used in combination with systematic instructional procedures'.

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Matcha, Uzir, Gasevic & Pardo 2020 is real (IEEE Trans Learn Technol 13(2):226-245, DOI 10.1109/TLT.2019.2916802), a systematic review of empirical LAD studies analysed against the Winne & Hadwin SRL model; the '29 studies' figure is confirmed (participant breakdown 5+9+4+11 = 29 papers; 22 student-facing, 18 teacher-facing, 10 both). What the summaries did not show: the specific findings the claim rests on (most dashboards not grounded in SRL theory, mostly peer comparison, little evidence of learning gains) or the proposed model of user-centred analytics across forethought/performance/reflection phases; only the review's motivation ('much less understanding how learning analytics are grounded in the literature on SRL') was visible. The substance is independently supported by Jivet et al. 2017 (see C13), which states that current designs foster competition rather than knowledge mastery and offer misguided frames of reference.
verdicts.corrected_source: Matcha W, Uzir NA, Gasevic D, Pardo A (2020) A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies on Learning Analytics Dashboards: A Self-Regulated Learning Perspective. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies 13(2):226-245.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: 29 papers confirmed; 22 dashboards student-facing, 18 teacher-facing, 10 both; 11 papers had >100 participants, 5 had 1-10. Findings on peer comparison and learning gains not visible in search summaries.

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Both sources are real: Jivet, Scheffel, Specht & Drachsler 2018, License to evaluate, LAK '18 pp. 31-40, DOI 10.1145/3170358.3170421 (Table 4 lists evaluation criteria assessed in the 26 included papers, so '26' is right); and Jivet et al. 2017, Awareness Is Not Enough, EC-TEL (95 papers met the first three criteria, only half had theoretical grounding, 26 analysed in depth, so '95' is right). The 2017 paper explicitly says current designs 'foster competition between learners rather than knowledge mastery, offering misguided frames of reference for comparison', which supports the warning about comparison frames. Not visible: the specific statement that comparison harms lower-performing learners' motivation, or the explicit recommendation to judge dashboards by learning/self-regulation effects rather than satisfaction. The 2018 review also reports mixed student preferences (Konert et al. liked peer comparison; Tabuenca et al. preferred personal analytics), which the claim omits.
verdicts.corrected_source: Jivet I, Scheffel M, Specht M, Drachsler H (2018) License to evaluate: Preparing learning analytics dashboards for educational practice. LAK '18, pp. 31-40. Jivet I, Scheffel M, Drachsler H, Specht M (2017) Awareness Is Not Enough: Pitfalls of Learning Analytics Dashboards in the Educational Practice. EC-TEL 2017, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-66610-5_7.
verdicts.corrected_numbers: 26 papers (2018) and 95 screened / 26 analysed (2017) both confirmed. 'Harms lower-performing learners' wording not seen; visible wording is 'foster competition ... misguided frames of reference for comparison'.

verdicts.notes: Two searches. Sibley et al. 2016 is real (J Consult Clin Psychol 84(8):699-712, PMID 27077693): STAND, 128 adolescents randomised, efficacy assessed at post-treatment and 6-month follow-up, conclusion 'acutely efficacious ... more work is needed to establish the nature of long-term effects', which is consistent with but not an explicit statement of the claim's 'gains faded by follow-up'. Not visible: ages 11-15, the '10 weekly sessions', or the outcome list (parent-rated symptoms, organisation, homework, conflict). Two material problems. First, STAND is described as targeting organisation, time management and planning plus 'parent-based monitoring and contingency management', i.e. it includes a reward/consequence component the claim's 'monitoring by agreement rather than nagging' description leaves out, which bears on the README's no-rewards stance. Second, the 2021 community trial (Sibley et al., JCCP, PMID 32861773; 278 adolescents, 82 therapists, 4 clinics, double randomisation) found NO significant group-by-time effects overall in intent-to-treat analysis versus usual care; STAND beat usual care only when delivered by licensed therapists (22% of the sample), and MI competence was lower than in university trials. 'Weaker when delivered by community clinicians' understates a null overall result.
verdicts.corrected_source: Sibley MH et al. (2016) Parent-teen behavior therapy + motivational interviewing for adolescents with ADHD. J Consult Clin Psychol 84(8):699-712. Sibley MH et al. (2021) Effectiveness of motivational interviewing-enhanced behavior therapy for adolescents with ADHD: a randomized community-based trial. J Consult Clin Psychol (PMID 32861773).
verdicts.corrected_numbers: 2016: n=128, post-treatment and 6-month follow-up, 'acutely efficacious'. 2021: n=278 adolescents, 82 therapists, ITT no significant overall effect vs usual care; benefit only with licensed therapists (22%); better parent participation, satisfaction and medication engagement. STAND includes contingency management.
